pron:man.tx: From Middle High German man, from Old High German man, from Proto-West Germanic *mann, from Proto-Germanic *mann- (“person”). Doublet of Mann. Cognate with English man, Dutch man, among many others (see the English entry for more).

adv:man.tx: From Middle Low German man, a contracting alteration of Old Saxon newan (“none other than”). Compare the similar case of Dutch maar (“only”).

adv:mal.tx: From the noun Mal (“time”). Partly shortened from einmal, which is also derived from the noun.

adj:mutig.tx: From Middle High German muotic, from Old High German muotag, from Proto-Germanic *mōdagaz; equivalent to Mut + -ig.

noun:Maus.tx: Inherited from Middle High German mūs, from Old High German mūs, from Proto-West Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs. Doublet of Mouse. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.

adv:mega.tx: From the prefix mega-, originally youth slang.

adj:mega.tx: From the prefix mega-, originally youth slang.

noun:Mittag.tx: From Middle High German mittetac, from Old High German mittitac, compound of mitti (see German Mitte) and tac (see Tag). Cognate to Dutch middag.

prep:mit.tx: From Middle High German mite, mit, from Old High German miti, mit, from Proto-West Germanic *midi. Cognate with German Low German met, mihe- (separable part of verbs) (Paderbornisch) and Middle English mid (“with”).

adv:mit.tx: From Middle High German mite, mit, from Old High German miti, mit, from Proto-West Germanic *midi. Cognate with German Low German met, mihe- (separable part of verbs) (Paderbornisch) and Middle English mid (“with”).

adj:müde.tx: From Middle High German müede, muode, from Old High German muodi, from Proto-West Germanic *mōþī. Cognate to Dutch moe.

noun:Menge.tx: From Middle High German menige, from Old High German managī, from Proto-Germanic *managį̄ (compare English many, Swedish många). Equivalent to manch + -e.

pron:mehr.tx: From Middle High German mēre, from Old High German mēro, from Proto-West Germanic *maiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *maizô, from Proto-Indo-European *mē- (“many”). See English more for more.

adv:mehr.tx: From Middle High German mēre, from Old High German mēro, from Proto-West Germanic *maiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *maizô, from Proto-Indo-European *mē- (“many”). See English more for more.

pron:mensch.tx: From Mensch (“human being”). Coined as (gender-neutral) alternative to man (“one”) for the same reason as frau, which see. Compare the use of they (vs she vs he) in English to refer to a generic or specific person whose gender is unknown.

noun:Manx.tx: From English Manx, from assumed Old Norse *manskr, an adjectival form of Mana, Mǫn (“Isle of Man”).

adj:mau.tx: Probably a blend of matt + flau, maybe with influence from mauen in the older sense of "to be weepy/annoying."

adv:mau.tx: Probably a blend of matt + flau, maybe with influence from mauen in the older sense of "to be weepy/annoying."

noun:Menschenaffe.tx: From Mensch (“man, human being, person”) + -en- + Affe (“ape”), cognate with Dutch mensaap.

adj:modern.tx: From French moderne, from Latin modernus.

adj:mild.tx: From Middle High German milte, from Old High German milti. The modern consonantism is Central and Low German; compare Middle Low German milde.

adj:malle.tx: From Low German mall, from Middle Low German mal, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Dutch mal.

noun:Moskito.tx: Borrowed from Spanish mosquito (“gnat”), diminutive of mosca (“fly”), from Latin musca (“fly”), from Proto-Indo-European *mūs- (“fly, stinging fly, gnat”).

noun:Mücke.tx: From Middle High German mücke, mügge, mucke, mugge, from Old High German mucka, mugga, from Proto-West Germanic *muggjā, from Proto-Germanic *mugjō, *muwō (“midge”), from Proto-Indo-European *mū- (“fly, midge”), *mu-, *mew-. Compare Dutch mug, Low German Mügg, Mügge, English midge, Danish myg, Latin musca.

noun:Mönch.tx: From Middle High German münch, münich, from Old High German munih, from Proto-West Germanic *munik.

noun:Mundart.tx: Compound of Mund (“mouth”) + Art (“nature, character”), already used by Justus-Georgius Schottelius (also known as Justus Georg Schottel) in his grammars (1641, 1663) and by Philippus Caesius (1641). Cognate to Dutch mondaard and Low German Mundort, Mundoort, Mundart, Mundaart, Swedish munart (rare).

verb:mieten.tx: From Middle High German, Old High German mieten. Synchronically analyzed as a verbal formation from Miete (“rent”).

noun:Manchester.tx: The fabric was primarily produced in Manchester.

noun:Mercedes-Benz.tx: From Mercedes + Benz, named after Mercédès Jellinek (daughter of Emil Jellinek, who commissioned the first Mercedes-Benz, the Mercedes 35 hp), and Karl Benz co-founder of Daimler-Benz (and founder of the forerunner Benz automotive company).

noun:Mandel.tx: From Middle High German mandel, from Old High German mandala, from Proto-West Germanic *mandalā (“almond”). Doublet of Amygdala and Mandorla.

noun:Mauser.tx: From Middle High German mūze, from Old High German mūzōn (“change, transform”), from Medieval Latin muta, from Latin mutare (“change, transform”).

noun:Marie.tx: Variant of Maria, or borrowed from French Marie.

noun:Mädchen.tx: From Middle High German magedichīn, meidichīn, from Old High German *magadihhīn or calqued from Middle Low German mēgedeken, megedekīn, both from Proto-West Germanic *magaþukīn. Equivalent to Magd + -chen.

noun:März.tx: Inherited from Middle High German merze.

noun:Mittwoch.tx: From Middle High German mittewoche, from Old High German mittawehha (literally “middle of the week”), calqued on Ecclesiastical Latin media hebdomas (whence Dalmatian misedma). Equivalent to Mitte (“mid, middle”) + Woche (“week”), becoming a masculine in Early Modern German after the other weekdays. Compare Middle Low German middewēke, English midweek. Originally meaning the middle between Sunday …

adj:matt.tx: From Middle High German mat, with influence from Old French mat (“in checkmate”), a clipping of French échec et mat (“checkmate”), and French mat (“matt; pale”).

noun:Meister.tx: From Middle High German meister, from Old High German meistar, from Proto-West Germanic *maistar (“master”). Doublet of Maestro, Magister, and Master.

noun:Montag.tx: From Middle High German mōntac, māntac, from Old High German mānotag (9th c.), māntag (12th c.), from Proto-West Germanic *mānini dag (“day of the moon”), equivalent to Mond + Tag. Compare Low German Maandag, Dutch maandag, English Monday, Danish mandag.

adv:meist.tx: From Old High German meist, from Proto-Germanic *maist, *maistaz. Compare Dutch meest, English most, Danish mest.

noun:Mineral.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin minerāle (neuter of minerālis), from Medieval Latin minera.

noun:Made.tx: From Middle High German made, from Old High German mado, from Proto-West Germanic *maþō. Originally a masculine; the feminine gender is of Central and Low German origin (Middle Low German māde f). Cognates Cognate with Dutch made, English maddock and maggot, Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌸𐌰 (maþa), Old Norse maðkr (Danish maddik).

noun:Madeleine.tx: Borrowed from French Madeleine. Doublet of Magdalena.

noun:Magister.tx: From Middle High German magister, from Old High German magister, a learned borrowing from Latin magister. Doublet of Maestro, Master, and Meister.

noun:Magnesium.tx: From New Latin magnēsium, from Ancient Greek μαγνησία (magnēsía), after Μαγνησία (Magnēsía, “Magnesia”).

noun:Magnet.tx: Borrowed from Latin magnēs (“lodestone”), from Ancient Greek μαγνῆτις [λίθος] (magnêtis [líthos], “Magnesian [stone]”), either after the Lydian city Magnesia ad Sipylum (modern-day Manisa, Turkey), or after the Greek region of Μαγνησία (Magnēsía) (whence came the colonist who founded the city in Lydia).

noun:Mai.tx: From Middle High German meie, from Old High German meio, from Latin (mensis) Maius, the Italic goddess of growth.

noun:Maid.tx: From Middle High German mait, meit, contracted form of Old High German maget, thus a doublet of Magd (“maid”). Cognates with Dutch meid, maagd, Low German Meid, Maagd, Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌲𐌰𐌸𐍃 (magaþs) and English maid.

noun:Mal.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German māl, from Proto-West Germanic *māl, from Proto-Germanic *mēlą. See also Mahl (“meal”), which is ultimately the same word. Cognate with English meal.

noun:Mandat.tx: Borrowed from Latin mandātum, from mandō (“to command”).

noun:Manga.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 漫画(まんが) (manga), from Middle Chinese 漫 (MC manH, “free, unrestrained”) + 畫 (MC hweaH|hweak, “drawing”).

noun:Mango.tx: From English mango, from Portuguese manga, from Malay mangga, from Tamil மாங்காய் (māṅkāy) from மா (mā, “mango species”) + காய் (kāy, “unripe fruit”).

noun:Mann.tx: From Middle High German man, from Old High German man, from Proto-West Germanic *mann, from Proto-Germanic *mann-, from Proto-Indo-European *mon-. Doublet of man.

noun:Mannequin.tx: Borrowed from French mannequin, from Dutch manneken.

noun:Marathon.tx: Borrowed from French marathon, from Ancient Greek Μαραθών (Marathṓn), perhaps from μάραθον (márathon, “fennel”), referring to the prevalence of the plant in the area.

noun:Mare.tx: From Latin mare with the plural maria. Doublet of Maar and Meer.

noun:Mark.tx: From Middle High German marc, marke.

noun:Maser.tx: From Middle High German maser, from Old High German masar, from Proto-West Germanic *masur (“veined wood”). Cognate to English mazer.

noun:Massage.tx: 19th century, from French massage. Analysable as massieren + -age.

noun:Mast.tx: From Middle High German mast, from Old High German mast, from Proto-West Germanic *mast.

noun:Master.tx: Borrowed from English master. Doublet of Maestro, Magister, and Meister.

noun:Material.tx: From Latin māteriālis. Doublet of materiell.

noun:Matrix.tx: Borrowed from Latin mātrīx. Doublet of Matrize.

noun:Maul.tx: From Middle High German mūl, mūle (“snout, mouth”), from Old High German *mūl, mūla (“snout”), from Proto-Germanic *mūlą, *mūlō (“muzzle, snout”), from Proto-Indo-European *mū- (“lips, muzzle”). Cognate with Dutch muil (“muzzle, snout”), Danish mule (“muzzle”), West Frisian mûle (“mouth”), Alemannic German Muul (“mouth”).

noun:Median.tx: Borrowed from English median, from Latin mediānus.

noun:Meer.tx: From Middle High German mere, mer, from Old High German meri, from Proto-West Germanic *mari. Doublet of Maar and Mare. Cognates Cognate with Dutch meer (“lake”), Low German Meer (“sea”), English mere (“sea, lake”). Via Indo-European is cognate with Latin mare.

noun:Mensch.tx: From Middle High German mensche, mensch, from Old High German mennisko, a substantivization of the adjective mennisk, from Proto-West Germanic *mannisk, from Proto-Germanic *manniskaz (“human”), from Proto-Germanic *mann- (“human, man”). Compare Yiddish מענטש (mentsh), Dutch mens, Danish menneske, Swedish människa, all with the primary sense of “person” or “human being”. The dialectal usage …

intj:Mensch.tx: From Middle High German mensche, mensch, from Old High German mennisko, a substantivization of the adjective mennisk, from Proto-West Germanic *mannisk, from Proto-Germanic *manniskaz (“human”), from Proto-Germanic *mann- (“human, man”). Compare Yiddish מענטש (mentsh), Dutch mens, Danish menneske, Swedish människa, all with the primary sense of “person” or “human being”. The dialectal usage …

noun:Merle.tx: From Middle High German merle, from Old High German merla, from Proto-West Germanic *merlā (“blackbird”). Doublet of Amsel (“blackbird”).

noun:Met.tx: From Middle High German mëte, from Old High German mëtu, from Proto-West Germanic *medu, from Proto-Germanic *meduz, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu (“honey, mead”). Compare Dutch mede, English mead, Danish mjød.

noun:Meteor.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin meteōrum, from Ancient Greek μετέωρον (metéōron), neuter of μετέωρος (metéōros, “up in the air”).

noun:Metro.tx: Borrowed from French métro, a clipping of métropolitain.

noun:Mett.tx: From Middle Low German met, from Old Saxon meti (“meal, dish”), from Proto-Germanic *matją, whence also Dutch met. Related with Proto-Germanic *matiz, whence English meat.

noun:Million.tx: 15th century, borrowed from Italian millione m. Feminine gender develops by analogy with other numbers as well as other nouns in -ion.

noun:Minister.tx: Borrowed from French ministre, from Latin minister.

noun:Minute.tx: 15th c., from Medieval Latin minūta (“60th of an hour; note”).

noun:Mission.tx: 16th century, learned borrowing from Latin missio. Later reinforced by cognate French mission.

noun:Mist.tx: From Middle High German mist, from Old High German mist, from Proto-West Germanic *mistu. Cognate with Dutch mest, Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍃𐍄𐌿𐍃 (maihstus).

intj:Mist.tx: From Middle High German mist, from Old High German mist, from Proto-West Germanic *mistu. Cognate with Dutch mest, Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍃𐍄𐌿𐍃 (maihstus).

noun:Model.tx: Borrowed from English model. Doublet of Modell.

noun:Monarchie.tx: Borrowed from Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía).

noun:Mond.tx: From Middle High German māne, from Old High German māno, from Proto-West Germanic *mānō. Later forms of the Middle High German word, mānde, had a final dental due to confusion with mānōt (“month”) (modern Monat). Cognates See also Dutch maan, English moon, Danish måne, Swedish måne, Icelandic máni; also Monat. Further Indo-European cognates: Latin mēnsis (“month”), Ancient Greek μήν (mḗn, …

noun:Monster.tx: Borrowed in the 18th century from English monster. Doublet of Monstrum.

noun:Montage.tx: 19th century, Unadapted borrowing from French montage.

noun:Moor.tx: From Middle Low German mōr, mūr, from Old Saxon mōr, from Proto-Germanic *mōraz, from Proto-Indo-European. Compare Dutch moer, English moor.

noun:Moratorium.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin morātōrium, nominalized neuter singular of morātōrius.

noun:Most.tx: From Middle High German most, from Old High German most, from Proto-West Germanic *must (“must”).

noun:Mulch.tx: Late-20th century, from English mulch. A rarity among the recent English borrowings in that has been adopted with a spelling pronunciation (which was quite common for older borrowings).

noun:Mull.tx: Byform of Müll (“waste, rubbish”, older also “earth, dust”), which see. Related with English mould (“loose earth”), but not directly cognate.

noun:Mullah.tx: Derived from Classical Persian مُلَّا (mullā), from Arabic مَوْلًى (mawlan, “vicar, guardian”).

noun:Mus.tx: From Middle High German muos, from Old High German muos, from Proto-West Germanic *mōs, from Proto-Germanic *mōsą.

noun:Museum.tx: Borrowed from Latin mūsēum (“library, study”), from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)).

noun:Musik.tx: From Middle High German mūsic, from Old High German musika, musica, from Latin mūsica (“music”).

noun:Muster.tx: 15th century, via Italian mostra (“exhibition”) (Vulgar Latin mōstra), from Latin mōnstrum (“omen”), linked to Latin monstrāre (“to show”) (Vulgar Latin mōstrāre). Cognate with English muster.

noun:Mutter.tx: From Middle High German muoter, from Old High German muoter, from Proto-West Germanic *mōder, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Compare Dutch moeder, English mother, Danish moder, Swedish moder.

noun:Meerschweinchen.tx: From Meer (“sea”) + Schwein (“pig, swine”) + -chen (diminutive suffix), literally “little sea pig”, or from Meerschwein + -chen. The use of Meer refers to the animal as coming from overseas.

noun:Milch.tx: From Middle High German milch, from Old High German miluh, from Proto-West Germanic *meluk, from Proto-Germanic *meluks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-.

noun:Mafioso.tx: Borrowed from Italian mafioso. Doublet of mafiös (adjective).

noun:Mogul.tx: Borrowed from English mogul. Doublet of Mongole.

noun:Mörser.tx: From Middle High German mörser, mörsære, from Old High German morsāri, from Proto-West Germanic *morsārī, alternative form of *mortārī (“mortar”). Doublet of Mörtel.

noun:Motte.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German motte, mutte, from Old Saxon *motta, from Proto-West Germanic *moþþā, perhaps related to *muggju (“mosquito, midge”), or *maþō (“worm”). Cognate with Dutch mot and English moth.

noun:Masche.tx: From Middle High German masche, from Old High German maska, from a Proto-West Germanic *maskā. Cognate with Old Saxon maska. More at mesh.

noun:Mangan.tx: From earlier Manganesium, from French manganèse.

verb:malen.tx: From Middle High German mālen, from Old High German mālōn, mālēn, denominative of māl (“spot, stain”), from Proto-West Germanic *mālijan, from Proto-Germanic *mēlijaną (compare Dutch maal), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“dark color”) (compare Lithuanian mė́las (“black”), Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “dark-colored, black”)).

verb:machen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German machen, from Old High German mahhōn, from Proto-West Germanic *makōn, from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“to knead, mix, make”). Cognate with Dutch maken, Low German maken, English make.

noun:Maulwurf.tx: From Middle High German mūlwurf, mūlwerf, which is composed of mūl (“mouth”) (see Maul) and wurf (“throwing”) (see werfen). This is a folk etymological reinterpretation of the earlier term moltwerf, from late Old High German mul(t)wurf, which actually meant "earth(up)thrower," the first element from molta (“earth, dust”) (see Molte). Thus, the original word referred to the mole as a creature that …

noun:Mühle.tx: From Middle High German mül(e), mülīn(e), from Old High German mulī, mulīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mulīnu (“mill”).

verb:meiden.tx: From Middle High German mīden, from Old High German mīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *mīþan. Cognate with Dutch mijden and Old English mīþan (archaic English mithe). The expected past forms in modern German would be *mitt, *gemitten (as still in leiden, schneiden), but the Grammatischer Wechsel was levelled out (perhaps to avoid the similarity with unrelated mit, mitten). To meiden was then …

noun:Muskat.tx: From Middle High German muscāt, from Old French muscate, from Medieval Latin (nux) muscāta (“nutmeg”), from muscātus (“musky”), from Late Latin muscus (“musk”), from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos, “musk”).

det:mein.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German mīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mīn. Compare English my and mine.

noun:Meile.tx: From Middle High German mīle, from Old High German mīla, ultimately from Latin mīlle.

adj:männlich.tx: From Middle High German manlich, from Old High German manlīh, manalīh, from Proto-West Germanic *mannlīk, from Proto-Germanic *mannlīkaz. By surface analysis, Mann + lich. Cognates include Dutch mannelijk, English manly, and Old Norse mannligr (“human”) (whence Danish mandlig, Swedish manlig).

adj:mager.tx: From Old High German magar, from Proto-Germanic *magraz, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. Cognate with Dutch mager, Danish mager, Norwegian Bokmål mager, Norwegian Nynorsk mager, Swedish mager, etc., and with English meagre (through Indo-European via Latin and French).

noun:Mittel.tx: From Middle High German mittel, from Old High German mittil (akin to Old Saxon middil), from Proto-Germanic *midlą, *midilą, *medalą (“middle”), *midil-. Compare Dutch middel, English middle. See also Mitte.

noun:Messer.tx: From Middle High German messer, mezzer, from Old High German mezzir, mezzeres, mezzirahs, mezzisahs (“knife”), from Proto-West Germanic *matisahs (“knife used for cutting food”).

verb:messen.tx: From Middle High German mëȥȥen, from Old High German mëȥȥen, from Proto-West Germanic *metan.

noun:Mausefalle.tx: From Middle High German mūsfalle, mūsvalle, from Old High German mūsfalla, from Proto-West Germanic *mūsfallā (“mousetrap”), equivalent to Maus + -e- + Falle. Cognate with German Low German Muusfalle, Muusfall (“mousetrap”), Dutch muizenval (“mousetrap”), Saterland Frisian Muusefalle (“mousetrap”), English mousefall (“mousetrap”).

noun:Moos.tx: From Middle High German mos, from Old High German mos, from Proto-Germanic *musą.

noun:Maulbeere.tx: From Middle High German mūlber(e), from Old High German mūlbere, a dissimilated variant of older mūrberi, from Proto-West Germanic *mūrubaʀi ~ *mōrubaʀi, from Latin mōrus.

noun:Mauer.tx: From Middle High German mūre, from Old High German mūra, from Proto-West Germanic *mūrā, from Latin mūrus, from Proto-Italic *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey-. Cognate with Yiddish מויער (moyer).

noun:Mähne.tx: From Middle High German mane, from Old High German mana, from Proto-West Germanic *manu, from Proto-Germanic *manō (“mane”), from Proto-Indo-European *mon- (“neck”). In Middle High German there existed a secondary variant man m, whence the plural mene. The modern form Mähne is from this plural (or from its merger with the original form mane). Cognate with English mane, which see.

noun:Müll.tx: An originally Central and Low German word from Middle Low German mül (“dust”) and Middle High German mülle, from Old High German mulli (“waste, rubbish”), a nominal formation from mullen (“to crush, grind”), from Proto-Germanic *muljaną (“to crush”) (DWDS).

noun:Moneten.tx: Borrowed from Latin monētae, plural of monēta, at first in grammar school slang, 18th c.

noun:Marder.tx: From Middle High German marder, from Old High German mardar, from Proto-West Germanic *marþr.

noun:Mantel.tx: From Middle High German mantel, from Old High German mantal, from Late Latin mantellum, diminutive of mantum, ultimately from Gaulish.

noun:Morgenstern.tx: From Middle High German morgenstern, from Old High German morganstern. Equivalent to Morgen + Stern.

noun:Morgen.tx: From Middle High German morgen, from Old High German morgan, from Proto-West Germanic *morgan, from Proto-Germanic *murganaz, from Proto-Indo-European *merkʷ- (“to blink, twinkle”). Compare Low German Morgen, Dutch morgen, West Frisian moarn, English morn, morrow, Danish morgen, Swedish morgon.

adv:morgen.tx: From Middle High German morgene, from Old High German morgane, from Proto-West Germanic *morgin, *murgin. Cognate with English morrow, morn.

noun:Möwe.tx: From Late Middle High German mēwe (Strasbourg, 1449), borrowed from Middle Dutch mêwe (along the Rhine) and Middle Low German mêwe (in East Prussia and along the Elbe), both from Proto-West Germanic *maiwā, from Proto-Germanic *maiwaz, which see. The bird was not entirely unknown in High German-speaking areas, but was restricted to the shores of the large rivers, along which it travels southwards …

noun:Meise.tx: From Middle High German meise, from Old High German meisa, from Proto-West Germanic *maisā, from Proto-Germanic *maisǭ (“chickadee”).

noun:Molch.tx: Alteration (with -ch) of Middle High German mol, molle, from Old High German mol, mol(l)o, from Proto-Germanic *mulô, from Proto-Indo-European *molh₂-o- (compare Lithuanian mul̃vas (“yellow, clayey”), Latin mulleus (“ruddy (shoes)”), Sanskrit मल (mála, “dirt”)), from *melh₂- (“dark color”). More at malen. Compare Luxembourgish Mouk.

noun:Mund.tx: From Middle High German munt, from Old High German mund, from Proto-West Germanic *munþ, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *men-. Cognate with Low German Mund, Dutch mond, English mouth, Danish mund.

noun:Muckefuck.tx: From Central Franconian Mucken (“brown earth”) + fuck (“foul, decayed”). A popular etymology derives the term from the French phrase moka faux (“false mocha”) but there is little to no evidence to support this explanation.

adj:melk.tx: From Middle High German melk, from Old High German melch, from Proto-West Germanic *melk, from Proto-Germanic *melkaz, ultimately from the root of Milch. Compare Old English þrimilce.

noun:Maas.tx: From Old High German Masa, from Proto-Germanic *Masō.

verb:missen.tx: From Middle High German missen, from Old High German missan, from Proto-Germanic *missijaną.

adj:marin.tx: Borrowed from Latin marīnus; cf. French marin.

noun:Mut.tx: From Middle High German muot, from Old High German muot, from Proto-West Germanic *mōd, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz. Cognate with Dutch moed, English mood.

verb:müssen.tx: From Middle High German müeȥen, from Old High German muoȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *mōtan. The preservation of the original diphthong can still be seen in Bavarian muass, the first and third person singular present form of miassn. See können for the origin of the historically unexpected umlaut.

adj:monumental.tx: From Late Latin monumentālis, via French monumental.

noun:Michel.tx: Popular form of Michael with reduction of unstressed syllables.

noun:Mohn.tx: With widespread dialectal -ā- → -ō- (as also in ohne and wo) from obsolete Mahn, from Middle High German māhe, māhen (Central German also already mān), from Old High German māho, from Proto-West Germanic *māhō, from Proto-Germanic *mēhô. Compare the variant Old High German mago. Cognate with Danish valmue, Swedish vallmo, Ancient Greek μήκων (mḗkōn) (Doric μάκων (mákōn)) and Old Church Slavonic …

noun:Maß.tx: From Middle High German māz, from Old High German māza, from Proto-West Germanic *mātu. Compare Dutch maat (“size, measure”), Old English met (“measure, amount, limit”). More at mete. Unrelated to Masse.

noun:Minze.tx: From Middle High German minze, from Old High German minza, from Proto-West Germanic *mintā (“mint”).

noun:Münze.tx: From Middle High German münze, from Old High German muniz, munizza, from Proto-West Germanic *munit.

noun:Monat.tx: From Middle High German mōnōt, mānōt m or n, from Old High German mānōd m, from Proto-West Germanic *mānōþ. See also Mond. Compare Old Saxon mānoth, Dutch maand, English month, Danish måned.

noun:Mitte.tx: From Middle High German mitte, from Old High German mitti, from Proto-Germanic *midjǭ (“centre”), *midją, from *midjaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *medʰyo-. Cognate to Old Norse miðja and Old English midde, midd (English mid).

adj:munter.tx: From Middle High German munter, from Old High German muntar, from Proto-West Germanic *mundr, from Proto-Germanic *mundraz.

verb:mögen.tx: From Middle High German mugen, from Old High German mugan, from Proto-West Germanic *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą, from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ-. Compare Dutch mogen, English may, Icelandic mega, Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌲𐌰𐌽 (magan), Serbo-Croatian moći, Bulgarian мога (moga). The modern sense of "like" developed out of a negated "nicht mögen", shifting from "to not be able to do" to "to not like doing" …

noun:Makel.tx: From Middle High German makel, borrowed from Latin macula. Related to Makulatur.

noun:Mehl.tx: From Middle High German mël (genitive mëlwes), from Old High German mëlo, from Proto-West Germanic *melu. Cognate with Dutch meel, English meal (“flour”).

noun:Meißel.tx: From Middle High German meizel, from Old High German meizil, from an original *meitil, from Proto-West Germanic *maitil, from Proto-Germanic *maitilaz.

adj:möglich.tx: From mögen + -lich; cognate with Hunsrik meeghlich, Dutch mogelijk.

noun:Markt.tx: From Middle High German market, from Old High German marchat, from Proto-West Germanic *markat (“market”).

noun:Muskel.tx: Ca. 1700, learned borrowing from Latin mūsculus. Doublet of Muschel. One of the few mixed-declension masculines in -el (cf. Pantoffel).

noun:Mord.tx: From Middle High German mort, from Old High German mord, from Proto-West Germanic *morþ, from Proto-Germanic *murþą. Cognate with Dutch moord, English murth, Swedish mord, Finnish murha. Also related with English murder, French meurtre.

noun:Magd.tx: From Middle High German maget, magt, from Old High German magad, from Proto-West Germanic *magaþ, from Proto-Germanic *magaþs. Cognates include Dutch meid, maagd, Low German Meid, Maagd, Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌲𐌰𐌸𐍃 (magaþs) and English maid.

noun:Macht.tx: From Middle High German maht, from Old High German maht. Cognate with Dutch macht, English might.

noun:Muße.tx: From Middle High German muoȥe, from Old High German muoȥa, derived from muoȥan (“to be able, to be allowed to”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōtan, from Proto-Germanic *mōtaną.

noun:Magen.tx: From Middle High German mage, from Old High German mago, from Proto-West Germanic *magō (“stomach”).

noun:Mahl.tx: The same word as Mal (“time”), from Middle High German māl, from Old High German māl, from Proto-West Germanic *māl. The sense “meal” developed from “mealtime” as also in cognate English meal. Further cognate with Dutch maal, Danish mål (“goal”). The orthographic distinction from Mal began in Early Modern German, probably in part under influence of etymology 2 below, which was then becoming …

noun:Makler.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German mākeler, mēkeler, and Middle Dutch makelare (compare modern Dutch makelaar). There are conflicting statements about whether the Dutch word was borrowed from Low German, or vice versa. The further origin is uncertain, but the word seems to be eventually derived from the verb Middle Low German māken, Middle Dutch maken (“to make”), from Old Saxon makōn or Old Dutch …

verb:mahnen.tx: From Middle High German mânen, from Old High German manōn, from Proto-Germanic *manōną. Cognate with Old English manian.

verb:mahlen.tx: From Middle High German maln, malen, from Old High German malan, from Proto-West Germanic *malan, from Proto-Germanic *malaną (“to grind”).

noun:Mangel.tx: Back-formation from mangeln (“to lack”). Related to Manko, which ultimately comes from the same source by way of a comparable derivation in Italian. Also related to English manque.

verb:mangeln.tx: From Old High German mangolōn, from Latin mancō.

pron:manch.tx: From Middle High German manec, from Old High German manag. The -ch is due to the traditional fricative pronunciation of non-initial -g- in Central German dialects. The spelling became predominant in Early New High German, possibly reinforced by the similar clusters in welch and solch. The original form has remained in mannigfach, manniglich, mannigfaltig, etc. Cognate with Dutch menig, English many, Polish mnogi.

noun:Märchen.tx: Diminutive of the noun Mär(e) f with -chen, compare Old High German māri (“news, tale”). Cognate with Luxembourgish Märchen.

noun:Masern.tx: 16th century, alteration of Maseln, borrowed from Middle Low German māselen. Cognate with Middle Dutch masel (“speckle”), whence modern Dutch mazelen (“measles”), and Old High German masala (“lump of blood”). The form with -r- through conflation with Maser (“vein or knob in wood”, etymology 2 below), which is probably related.

noun:Matrose.tx: Borrowed from Dutch matroos + -e, from Middle French matelots, from Old French matenot (“sailor, bunkmate”), most likely from Middle Dutch mattenoot (“bunk fellow”) or less likely Old Norse mǫtunautr (“food companion”).

noun:Meineid.tx: From Middle High German meineit, from Old High German meineid, from Proto-West Germanic *mainaiþ, from Proto-Germanic *mainaiþaz.

verb:meinen.tx: From Middle High German meinen, from Old High German meinen, from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną (“to mean, think; lament”). Germanic cognates include Dutch menen, Middle Low German meinen, mênen (whence Swedish mena etc.), West Frisian miene, English mean. Also related with English moan. Indo-European cognates include Old Irish mían and Czech mínit.

noun:Mütze.tx: From Middle High German almuʒ, ultimately from Medieval Latin almutia (“hood, cowl”), of unknown origin. Compare Latin amictus (“clothed, veiled”).

noun:Müller.tx: From Middle High German mülnære, from Old High German mulināri.

noun:Milz.tx: From Middle High German milze n, from Old High German milzi n, from Proto-Germanic *miltiją n. The feminine gender in modern German is from Middle Low German milte f, reinforced by the analogy with other inner organs. Cognate to Dutch milt, English milt.

noun:Mehltau.tx: From Middle High German miltau, from Old High German miltau, from militou, from Proto-West Germanic *milidauw, from Proto-Germanic *milidawwaz; equivalent to *mili (“honey”) + *dawwō (“dew”). The modern form through a secondary coincidence with Mehl (“flour”), which is due to the regular vocalic development in Low German and some dialects of Central German; compare Middle Low German mēldouwe, from Old Saxon milidou.

noun:Messe.tx: Inherited from Middle High German messe, from Old High German missa, itself from Latin missa.

noun:Messing.tx: From Middle High German messinc, from Proto-West Germanic *massing.

noun:Metzger.tx: From Middle High German metziger, metzigære, variants of metzjer, metzjære, from Old High German meziāri, mezziāri (“butcher”), from Proto-West Germanic *mattjārī. Perhaps influenced by Old High German mezalāri, mezzilāri (“merchant, moneychanger, butcher”), from Latin macellārius (“meat trader”).

noun:Mieder.tx: From Middle High German müeder, from Old High German muodar.

noun:Miene.tx: Borrowed from French mine (“appearance; expression”), itself from Breton min (“beak, muzzle”).

noun:Miete.tx: From Middle High German miete, from Old High German mieta, from Proto-West Germanic *miʀdu (“reward”).

noun:Mistel.tx: From Middle High German mistel f or m, from Old High German mistil m, from Proto-West Germanic *mistil, from Proto-Germanic *mistilaz m.

noun:Möbel.tx: 15th century, from Middle French meuble(s) (“household goods”), from Latin mobilis. At first restricted to the Moselle region, more widely attested since ca. 1600. Doublet of mobil. Cognate with Hunsrik Mevel.

noun:Möhre.tx: From Middle High German morhe, morche, from Old High German morha, from Proto-West Germanic *morhā, from Proto-Germanic *murhǭ. Cognate with obsolete English more (“carrot, parsnip”).

noun:Mühe.tx: From Middle High German müeje, müe, from Old High German muohī, from the root of the verb mühen (“to toil”). Cognate with Hunsrik Mih.

noun:Minne.tx: Borrowed in the Romantic era from Middle High German minne, from Old High German minna (“loving remembrance”); from Proto-West Germanic *minnju, from Proto-Germanic *minjō.

noun:Martini.tx: Borrowed from Latin Martini, genitive of Latin Martinus (“Martin”).

verb:mähen.tx: From Middle High German mæjen, mæwen, from Old High German māen, from Proto-West Germanic *māan. Cognate with English mow.

verb:melden.tx: From Middle High German mëlden, from Old High German mëldōn, mëldēn, from Proto-West Germanic *melþōn.

verb:melken.tx: From Middle High German mëlken, from Old High German melchan, from Proto-West Germanic *melkan, from Proto-Germanic *melkaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-. The consonantism -lk- is regular High German. The difference between melken and Milch is due to the fact that the latter used to have a short vowel after -l- (Old High German miluh). Compare Dutch melken, English milk, Danish malke, Norwegian mjølke.

verb:merken.tx: From Middle High German merken, from Old High German merchen, from Proto-West Germanic *markijan, from Proto-Germanic *markijaną (“to mark, notice”). Cognate with Dutch merken and Icelandic merkja.

verb:mischen.tx: From Middle High German mischen (“to mix”) from Old High German misken (“to mix”), from Proto-West Germanic *miskijan (“to mix”). Akin to English to mix, Bavarian mischn (“to mix”), Middle Low German mischen (“to mix”).

noun:Marmelade.tx: 16th century, from Middle French marmelade, from Portuguese marmelada.

noun:Melone.tx: Borrowed roughly simultaneously (15th c.) in the south from Italian melone, in the north through Middle Low German melōne and Middle Dutch meloen from Middle French melon. Both from Late Latin mēlō, shortening of Latin mēlopepō, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn, literally “ripe fruit”).

noun:Möglichkeit.tx: From Middle High German mügelichheit, mügelichkeit. By surface analysis, möglich (“possible”) + -keit (“-ness, -ity”). Compare Alemannic German Möglichkeit, Luxembourgish Méiglechkeet, Dutch mogelijkheid, Swedish möjlighet.

prep:mangels.tx: From genitive singular of Mangel (“lack”). Compare betreffs (“in regards to”), from genitive singular of Betreff (“subject (of an email)”).

verb:minen.tx: Borrowed from French miner or denominal Mine + -en.

verb:muten.tx: From Middle High German muoten, from Old High German muoten, muotôn.

noun:Metall.tx: From Middle High German metalle, from Latin metallum (14th century).

noun:Mittelalter.tx: From Middle High German mittel alter (“middle age [of life]”), at least since the 16th century also univerbated. By surface analysis, mittel- (“mid, middle”) + Alter (“age”). The historic sense dates from the 18th century and is a calque of New Latin medium aevum, from the idea that it was the interim between Antiquity and Modernity.

prep:mang.tx: From northern Middle High German manc, inmanc and Middle Low German manc (“among”). Related with German mengen, English among.

noun:Mette.tx: From Middle High German mettī, from Old High German mattina, a borrowing of Late Latin mattina from Classical Latin (laudēs) mātūtīnae (“morning (praise)”).

noun:Minna.tx: Popularized by the comedy Minna von Barnhelm (1767) by G. E. Lessing, see quotations.

adj:maskulin.tx: In the grammatical sense (since 15th c.) from Latin masculīnus. Broader use (chiefly since 19th c.) after French masculin.

noun:Marienkäfer.tx: From Marien- (cf. genitive forms: Mariens, Mariä, Marias, der Maria (i.e. of the Mary)), a bound morpheme derived from Maria (“Maria, Mary”); Käfer (“beetle”). Compare ladybird and ladybug, where “lady” refers to the Virgin Mary.

noun:Maschine.tx: Borrowed from French machine (“machine”), from Latin māchina.

noun:Machete.tx: Borrowed from Spanish machete with a spelling pronunciation.

noun:Munition.tx: From French munition, from Latin mūnitiō (“a defence, fortification”).

noun:Müsli.tx: Borrowed from Alemannic German Müesli, diminutive of Mues, itself cognate to German Mus and English mush (“stew, pottage”).

noun:Muschel.tx: From Middle High German muschel, from Old High German muscula, from Proto-West Germanic *muskulā (“mussel”). Doublet of Muskel.

noun:Muttersprache.tx: Loan translation and/or phonetic adaptation of Middle Low German môdersprâke, itself possibly a loan translation of Latin lingua materna. Analyzable as Mutter (“mother”) + Sprache (“language”).

noun:Minirock.tx: From Mini (“mini”) + Rock (“skirt”), probably a calque of English miniskirt.

noun:Mammut.tx: From French mammouth, from Russian ма́монт (mámont, “mammoth”).

verb:mutmaßen.tx: From Middle High German muotmāȥen, a verbal formation from muotmāȥe. Synchronically analyzed as Mut (“courage, mood”) + messen (“to measure”).

noun:Mumie.tx: 16th century, from Italian mummia, from Arabic, from Persian مومیا (mumiyâ).

adj:meschugge.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish משוגע (meshuge, “crazy”). Compare English meshugge and mishegoss.

noun:Maurer.tx: From Middle High German mūrære, from Old High German mūrāri. By surface analysis, Mauer (“wall”) + -er.

noun:Moschee.tx: Borrowed from French mosquée, from Italian moschea, ultimately from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid, literally “place of prostration”).

noun:Makrele.tx: From Middle High German makrēle, from Middle Low German makkerēle, from Middle Dutch makereel, from Old French maquerel. Further origin unknown. Compare modern Dutch makreel, modern French maquereau, English mackerel.

noun:Moloch.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin moloch, from Hebrew מולך.

noun:Meiler.tx: From Middle High German mīler, from Medieval Latin miliarium (“a quantity of a thousand pieces”), referring to the layers of logs built up to form the kiln, from Latin mille (“thousand”).

noun:Meinung.tx: From Middle High German meinunge, from Old High German meinunga. By surface analysis, meinen + -ung. Compare Dutch mening and English meaning.

adj:mächtig.tx: From Middle High German mähtec (mähtic, mehtec, mehtic), from Old High German mahtīg, mahtīc, from Proto-West Germanic *mahtīg. Equivalent to Macht + -ig. Compare Dutch machtig, English mighty.

noun:Mokka.tx: Borrowed from French moka or English mocha.

noun:Millionär.tx: Borrowed from French millionnaire. Equivalent to Million + -är.

noun:Meerrettich.tx: From Middle High German merretich, from Old High German meriratih; compare Dutch mierik (from Middle Dutch meerrâdic). By surface analysis, Meer (“sea”) + Rettich (“radish”), from the use of Meer to mean “foreign”, as also in Meerkatze, Meerschweinchen. The fact that horseradish is most often eaten in Germany with fish is coincidental, though speakers may make that connection. Alternative …

noun:Mirakel.tx: From Late Middle High German mirākel, from Latin miraculum.

noun:Malz.tx: From Middle High German malz, from Old High German malz, from Proto-Germanic *maltą (“malt”).

noun:Matte.tx: From Middle High German matte, from Old High German matta, from Late Latin matta, from a Semitic language.

noun:Mörder.tx: From Middle High German morder, mordære (also Middle High German morderære), from Old High German murdiro, murdreo (“murderer”), from Proto-Germanic *murþrijô (“murderer”). By surface analysis, morden + -er, or Mord + -er.

adj:mörderisch.tx: Mörder + -isch, since the 15th century. Compare also Middle High German mordisch, mördisch.

noun:Molotowcocktail.tx: From Molotow (surname of Vyacheslav Molotov) + Cocktail, a calque of Finnish Molotovin koktaili. Coined during the Winter War (1939/40) and first attested in German in the early 1940s.

noun:Magazin.tx: From Italian magazzino (“warehouse”), from Arabic مَخْزَن (maḵzan, “warehouse”) and its plural مَخازِن (maḵāzin). The military senses are from French magasin, the sense “periodical” from English magazine, both from the same Italian and Arabic sources.

verb:mengen.tx: From Middle High German mengen, from Old High German mengen, from Proto-West Germanic *mangijan, from Proto-Germanic *mangijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *monk-éye-ti, from Proto-Indo-European *menk- (“to press, knead”). Cognates include Dutch mengen and English ming, meng, mingle.

noun:Marone.tx: Borrowed from French marron or Italian marrone.

noun:Masse.tx: From Middle High German masse, from Late Old High German massa, from Latin massa.

noun:Memoiren.tx: Borrowed from French mémoires, plural of mémoire.

noun:Musiker.tx: 18th century, from Musik + -er, after Musikus, which it has displaced.

noun:Mitleid.tx: From Middle High German mitelīden, first used in mystic literature as a calque of Latin compassiō (“compassion”), itself a calque of Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia, “compassion, sympathy”). By surface analysis, mit (“with”) + Leid (“sorrow, suffering”). From Middle High German is borrowed Dutch medelijden.

verb:maskieren.tx: From French masquer + -ieren. By surface analysis, Maske + -ieren.

noun:Milliarde.tx: 18th century, borrowed from French milliard m. Feminine gender after Million.

noun:Milliardär.tx: Borrowed from French milliardaire. Equivalent to Milliarde + -är.

noun:Maskottchen.tx: From Maskotte (rare) + -chen, in origin a diminutive; from French mascotte.

noun:Monsun.tx: Borrowed from English monsoon, from Portuguese monção, from Arabic مَوْسِم (mawsim). Attested since the 17th century, in common use since the 19th.

noun:Marzipan.tx: Borrowed from Italian marzapane. See English marzipan for more.

noun:Medizin.tx: From Old French medecine, from Latin medicīna.

noun:Mitgefühl.tx: From mit- + Gefühl. Cognate with Dutch medegevoel.

noun:Mitgift.tx: From Middle High German mitegift (“dowry”). By surface analysis, mit- + Gift; the latter word here has the sense “gift; donation”.

noun:Medaille.tx: Borrowed from French médaille, from Italian medaglia, from Latin metallum.

noun:Mehrheit.tx: Calque of Dutch meerderheid (1719), itself probably a calque (± 1600) of French pluralité (“majority”), originating 1559. Old High German mērheit (“quality of being more”) had no attested continuation. Analyzable as mehr (“more”) + -heit (“-hood”).

noun:Mandoline.tx: From French mandoline, from Italian mandolino, diminutive of mandola.

noun:Menü.tx: Borrowed from French menu. Doublet of Minute. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English menu, itself from the French.

noun:Methode.tx: Borrowed from Latin methodus f, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).

noun:Militär.tx: Borrowed from French militaire, from Latin mīlitāris (“of a soldier or the military”). First attested in the 18th century.

noun:Masochismus.tx: Masoch + -ismus, the former named after Austrian novelist Leopold von Sacher-Masoch. Masoch may be a Germanized form of a lost Slavic placename, as Poland and Ukraine used to be part of the Austro-Hungarian empire.

noun:Mechanismus.tx: Learned borrowing from New Latin mechanismus, from Ancient Greek μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine”).

noun:Makake.tx: Borrowed from French macaque, from Portuguese macaco, of uncertain origin.

noun:Meteorologie.tx: 17th century, from Ancient Greek μετεωρολογία (meteōrología), in part through French météorologie, equivalent to meteoro- + -logie.

noun:Manege.tx: Borrowed from French manège, from Italian maneggio, from maneggiare.

noun:Majoran.tx: From Middle High German maiorān, from Late Old High German maiolan, from Medieval Latin maiorana (“majoranus”).

noun:Manier.tx: From Middle High German maniere, borrowed from Old French maniere, derived from Latin manuārius.

verb:massieren.tx: Borrowed from French masser, probably from Arabic مَسَّ (massa, “to touch”), or from Portuguese amassar. The Arabic verb was, in French, associated with and perhaps reinforced by unrelated Ancient Greek μάσσειν (mássein, “to knead”), but direct derivation from this latter is now considered unlikely.

noun:Macher.tx: From Middle High German macher, from Old High German mahhāri. By surface analysis, machen (“to make”) + -er (agent suffix). Cognates include Dutch maker, English maker and, via Yiddish מאַכער (makher), English macher.

noun:Miesmuschel.tx: First attested in the 18th century. The first syllable is of uncertain origin.

verb:missbrauchen.tx: From Middle High German missebrūchen, from Old High German missibrūchen, missibrūhhen, from Proto-Germanic *missabrūkaną, equivalent to miss- + brauchen. Cognate with German Low German missbruken, Dutch misbruiken, West Frisian misbrûke, Saterland Frisian misbruuke, Danish misbruge, Swedish missbruka.

adj:merkwürdig.tx: merken (“to notice, to mark”) + -würdig (“-worthy”). Compare Dutch merkwaardig and English markworthy.

verb:meckern.tx: Iterative of mecken, of imitative origin; compare Latin micciō (“to bleat”), Sanskrit मेक (meka, “goat”), Ancient Greek μηκάς (mēkás, “goat”).

adv:morgens.tx: From Middle High German morgens, morgenes, adverbial genitive of morgen, whence modern German Morgen (“morning”). Equivalent to Morgen + -s.

noun:Meuterei.tx: 16th century, probably from Dutch muiterij, from Middle Dutch muiterie (attested 1350), eventually derived from Old French meute, whence also German Meute. The Middle Dutch itself might be from Middle French meuterie, which, however, is later and generally rare. While the Middle French is given by several German dictionaries as the etymon of Meuterei, most Dutch dictionaries consider Middle Dutch …

verb:meutern.tx: Back-formation from Meuterei. Analysable as Meute + -ern.

noun:Maniküre.tx: 20th-century borrowing from French manicure, variant of modern French manucure, modeled after older pédicure from Latin manus (“hand”) + cūra (“care”).

noun:Mangold.tx: From Middle High German man(e)golt. Further origin unknown. A relation with the personal name below suggests itself phonetically, but is semantically nebulous.

noun:Mannschaft.tx: From Middle High German manschaft; analysable as Mann (“man”) + -schaft (“-hood, -ship”). Compare English manship.

verb:meucheln.tx: 16th century, possibly inherited from Middle High German *miucheln, *mūcheln, from Old High German *mūhhilōn, iterative of mūhhōn (“to lurk, ambush”), from Proto-Germanic *mūkōną. The earlier existence of the iterative verb is ascertained by derivatives such as Middle High German miucheler, mūcheler, Old High German mūhhilāri (“bandit”). The modern form is either an unattested inheritance or a …

adj:makaber.tx: From French macabre, through Spanish macabro and possibly Arabic مَقَابِر (maqābir, “cemeteries”), plural of مَقْبَرَة (maqbara).

noun:Murmel.tx: Inherited from Old High German murmul, byform with vowel assimilation of marmul, itself by liquid dissimilation from Latin marmor (“marble”). Doublet of Marmor.

noun:Marmor.tx: Borrowed from Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble, crystalline rock”). Doublet of Murmel.

adj:materiell.tx: Borrowed from French matériel, from Latin māteriālis. Doublet of Material.

noun:Monteur.tx: 19th century, from French monteur. Equivalent to montieren + -eur.

noun:Molke.tx: From Middle High German molken, from Proto-West Germanic *molknu (“dairy product, curdled milk”). Cognate with Middle Dutch molken, Old Saxon molken, Old English molcen. Related with German melken, but details are unclear.

noun:Morgenland.tx: Morgen (“East”, literally “morning”) + Land (“land”). First attested in the Luther Bible as a translation of Ancient Greek ἀνατολή (anatolḗ).

noun:Münster.tx: From Middle High German münster, from Old High German munistiuri (8th century), from Vulgar Latin *monisterium, from Latin monastērium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion). Cognate with English minster and the doublet monastery, and Sicilian misteri.

noun:Modell.tx: Borrowed from Italian modello. Doublet of Model.

noun:Misere.tx: Borrowed from French misère, from Latin miseria.

adj:manuell.tx: Borrowed from French manuel (“manual”), from Latin manualis, from manus (“hand”).

intj:moin.tx: From, or from the same source as, German Low German moin, beyond which the etymology is not clear; see that entry for more.

adj:müßig.tx: From Middle High German müeȥic, müeȥec, from Old High German muoȥīg, from Proto-West Germanic *mōtīg (“opportune”), from *mōtijan (“to have opportunity”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōtā (“opportunity”). By surface analysis, Muße + -ig.

noun:Murmeltier.tx: From Middle High German murmeltier (14th c.), folk-etymological alteration as murmeln (“to murmur”) + Tier (“animal”) of older murmendīn, from Old High German murmunto (probably through a diminutive *murmuntīn), from Latin mūrem montis (accusative, literally “mountain rat”). Compare English marmot.

noun:Maxime.tx: From French maxime, from Latin maximē.

verb:murren.tx: Of imitative origin. Compare murmeln, Swedish morra.

noun:Meldung.tx: melden + -ung, cognate with Dutch melding, Icelandic melding, Norwegian Bokmål melding, and Norwegian Nynorsk melding.

noun:Melodie.tx: From Middle High German melodīe, from Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā). Since the 16th century, the inherited form Melodei was increasingly readapted to the Latin and to French mélodie.

adj:mütterlich.tx: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mōdērlīkaz (“motherly, maternal”). By surface analysis, Mutter + -lich.

adj:meliert.tx: From French mêlé + -iert or past participle of melieren.

adj:melancholisch.tx: From Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós, “atrabilious, impulsive, of atrabilious or melancholic temperament”), from μελαγχολία (melankholía, “melancholy”). By surface analysis, Melancholie + -isch.

noun:Mohr.tx: From Middle High German mōr, mōre, Old High German Mōr, from Latin Maurus, 8th c.

verb:mixen.tx: Borrowed from English mix, from Middle English mixen, partially inherited from Old English mixen, and partially from a backformation of Old French mixte, itself a borrowing from Latin mixtus, past participle of miscere. Doublet of mischen.

adj:mexikanisch.tx: From Mexiko + -isch with -an- from -ānus and analogy.

adj:mäßig.tx: From Middle High German, from Old High German; equivalent to Maß + -ig.

noun:Mitra.tx: From Latin mitra, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra, “headband, turban”).

noun:Mietwagen.tx: Compound of mieten (“to hire/to rent”) + Wagen (“car”).

noun:Mio.tx: Spelling pronunciation of the abbreviation Mio or Mio.. See Etymology 1.

noun:Musikant.tx: 16th century, from Medieval Latin mūsicāns, present participle of mūsicō (“to play music”), perhaps through Italian musicante. Equivalent to Musik + -ant.

verb:marodieren.tx: From French marauder + -ieren. Cognate to German marode.

noun:Matratze.tx: From Middle High German materaz, from Old French materas, from Arabic مَطْرَح (maṭraḥ). The modern German form was influenced by older Italian materazzo and/or Medieval Latin matracium, from the same Arabic source. (The Old French form may have been borrowed via Italian, too.)

noun:Maßnahme.tx: From the verb maßnehmen (“to take measure”).

noun:Maut.tx: A Bavarian word, from Middle High German mūte, from Old High German mūta, borrowed from Gothic 𐌼𐍉𐍄𐌰 (mōta), from Proto-Germanic *mōtō. Cognate with Old English mōt and Swedish muta

noun:Myriade.tx: Borrowed from English myriad, originally in the plural form Myriaden, from a translation of Paradise Lost.

adj:machiavellistisch.tx: From the family name of the Italian philosopher Niccolò Machiavelli.

noun:Mitternacht.tx: Inherited from Middle High German mitternaht, from Old High German mittinaht, from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts.

verb:misslingen.tx: Middle High German misselingen, Old High German missilingan

adj:missverständlich.tx: From missverstehen + -lich. By surface analysis, miss- + verständlich

adv:missverständlich.tx: From missverstehen + -lich. By surface analysis, miss- + verständlich

adv:mittlerweile.tx: From (in) mittler Weile. Compare Dutch inmiddels.

verb:meistern.tx: From Middle High German meistern, from Old High German meistarōn. Equivalent to Meister + -n.

noun:Mahlzeit.tx: 15th century, from Mahl (“meal”) + Zeit (“time”). The word Mahl (a spelling variant of Mal) originally meant "mealtime", but was transferred to the meal itself. The compound then assumed the sense "mealtime", but ultimately underwent the same semantic development yet again. Compare Dutch maaltijd, English mealtide, Danish måltid, Icelandic máltíð.

intj:Mahlzeit.tx: 15th century, from Mahl (“meal”) + Zeit (“time”). The word Mahl (a spelling variant of Mal) originally meant "mealtime", but was transferred to the meal itself. The compound then assumed the sense "mealtime", but ultimately underwent the same semantic development yet again. Compare Dutch maaltijd, English mealtide, Danish måltid, Icelandic máltíð.

verb:mogeln.tx: Unknown, perhaps related to maucheln, variant of meucheln.

noun:Möse.tx: Uncertain, perhaps from thieves' cant Moß, Muß (“woman”), influenced by late Middle High German mutze (“vulva”).

noun:Mieter.tx: From Middle High German mietære. By surface analysis, mieten + er.

intj:menno.tx: Variation of manno, clipping of Mannomann, emphatic form of the interjection Mann.

adj:mondsüchtig.tx: From Mondsucht (literally “moon illness”) + -ig. Also analysable as Mond + süchtig, literally “addicted to the moon”, but this is not the original interpretation.

verb:morden.tx: From Middle High German morden, mörden, mürden, from Old High German morden, murden, from Proto-West Germanic *murþijan, from Proto-Germanic *murþijaną. The form was continuously readapted to the noun. Equivalent to Mord + -en.

noun:Minarett.tx: Borrowed from French minaret, ultimately from Arabic مَنَارَة (manāra).

verb:masturbieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin masturbāri, with the verbal ending adapted as -ieren.

noun:Mischung.tx: From Middle High German mischunge, from Old High German miskunga. By surface analysis, mischen + -ung.

noun:Mosaik.tx: 15th century, from Italian mosaico m, from Medieval Latin musaicum n. Common since 18th century after French mosaïque f, itself from the Italian.

noun:Manometer.tx: Borrowed from French manomètre, formed from Ancient Greek μανός (manós, “thin, rare”) + μέτρον (métron).

intj:Manometer.tx: A fanciful extension of Mann on the basis of the above term.

noun:Maßstab.tx: 15th century, from Maß (“measure”) + Stab (“staff”). Compare Dutch maatstaf.

noun:Mörtel.tx: From Middle High German mörter, mortel, from Old High German mortāri, *mortāli, from Proto-West Germanic *mortārī, *mortālī (“mortar”). Doublet of Mörser.

verb:mitteilen.tx: From Middle High German mite teilen, corresponding to mit- + teilen.

noun:Metonymie.tx: From Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

noun:Milbe.tx: From Middle High German milwe, milewe, from Old High German miliwa. Cognate with archaic Dutch meluw (“woodlouse”), Middle Low German mēle (“mite”). Further related with German mahlen (“to grind”), Mehl (“flour”), English meal (“coarse flour”). Also compare Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌻𐍉 (malō, “moth”) and Swedish mal (“moth”), which could be related.

noun:Maracuja.tx: Borrowed from Portuguese maracujá, from Old Tupi murukuîá.

verb:murmeln.tx: From a Proto-Indo-European *mur- (“to murmur”), which appears to be onomatopoeic; see Latin murmur (“murmur”) for more cognates. Note also murren (“to grumble”).

adj:muskulär.tx: Borrowed from French musculaire. By surface analysis, Muskel + -är.

noun:Mittelstand.tx: From mittel- (“middle, central”) + Stand (“stand(ing), position, estate”); perfectly parallel to cognate Dutch middenstand.

adv:meinetwegen.tx: Shortened from von meinetwegen, which can be traced through two developmental routes. One route is from von meinentwegen / von meinent wegen, from von meinen wegen, from Middle High German von mînen wëgen, in which wegen was the dative plural of modern-day Weg and mînen was the possessive pronoun in the dative plural. Another route can be traced from von meintwegen / von meint wegen, from Middle …

verb:mitkommen.tx: mit- (“with”) + kommen (“to come”); cognate with Hunsrik mitkomme

adj:mannigfaltig.tx: From Middle High German manecvaltec, from Old High German manicfaltīg, from Proto-Germanic *managafalþaz, equivalent to manch + faltig. Compare English manifold.

noun:Multiversum.tx: Coined by German philosopher Heinrich Rickert, analogous to Universum.

noun:Monolog.tx: Borrowed from French monologue, from Ancient Greek μονόλογος (monólogos).

noun:Mündel.tx: From the obsolete Mund (“hand, legal protection”)

noun:Maultier.tx: From Middle High German *mūltier, from Old High German *mūltior, from Proto-West Germanic *mūladeuʀ, from *mūl + *deuʀ. Equivalent to obsolete Maul (“mule”) + Tier (“animal”). Cognate with Dutch muildier.

noun:Mieze.tx: Possibly onomatopoeic — according to Duden, derived from a beckoning call for cats, “mi”, optionally reduplicated as “mi-mi(-mi)”. Compare against Albanian mace (“cat”), French matou (“tomcat”), and Proto-Slavic *maca (“pussycat”).

adv:miteinander.tx: From Middle High German miteinander. Equivalent to mit- + einander.

noun:Messias.tx: Borrowed from Latin Messīās, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Μεσσίας (Messías), from Aramaic משיחא (məšīḥā), from Biblical Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšîaḥ, “anointed”).

noun:Meier.tx: First attested as Old High German meior (9th century). Middle High German meier or meiger. Ultimately from Medieval Latin maior (domus).

adj:monoton.tx: 18th century, borrowed from French monotone, from Late Latin monotonus, from Ancient Greek μονότονος (monótonos). By surface analysis, mono- + Ton.

verb:mitmachen.tx: From mit- + machen. Cognate with Hunsrik mitmache.

noun:Marschall.tx: From Middle High German marschalc (“officer in charge of the royal horse stables”), from Old High German marahscalc (“groom; ostler”). Equivalent to Mähre (“mare”) + Schalk (“rogue”). The modern word has been influenced, both phonetically and semantically, by French maréchal, from Old French mariscal, itself of Germanic origin and hence etymologically the same word.

noun:Muräne.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin mūraena, mūrēna, from Ancient Greek μύραινα (múraina). Attested since the 14th century, sometimes also borrowed as Mure (18th century). Not related to German Maräne.

adj:melodiös.tx: Borrowed from French mélodieux, equivalent to Melodie + -ös.

noun:Materialismus.tx: From English materialism, perhaps via French.

noun:Manuskript.tx: 16th century, borrowed from Medieval Latin manuscrīptum.

adv:mitnichten.tx: Univerbation of mit (“with”) + nichten (“nothing”), a now-obsolete byform of nichts and nicht. Attested by the 15th century, separated spelling goes back to Middle High German.

adj:mausetot.tx: Borrowed from Low German mursdōd, interpreting mu(r)s (“suddenly, entirely”) as Mūs (“mouse”) (New High German Maus) through folk etymology. Compare Dutch morsdood.

noun:Major.tx: 16th century, probably borrowed from Spanish mayor, from Latin maior.

noun:Mädel.tx: Same as Mädchen with a different diminutive suffix. Equivalent to Magd + -el.

noun:Mesosphäre.tx: From Ancient Greek μέσος (mésos, “middle of, between”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, sphere”).

adj:mündig.tx: From Middle High German mündec, derived from munt, from Proto-Germanic *mundō. Compare Vormund, mundtot.

adv:mithin.tx: 16th century, from mit (“with”) + hin (“thither”), at first meaning “at that time, at once”.

noun:Mitochondrium.tx: Coined by German microbiologist Carl Benda in 1898, from Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread”) + χονδρίον (khondríon), diminutive of χόνδρος (khóndros, “grain, morsel”).

noun:Megabyte.tx: Borrowed from English megabyte; mega- + Byte.

noun:Mitose.tx: From Ancient Greek μίτος (mítos, “thread”) + -ose. Coined by Walther Flemming in 1879.

noun:Mumpitz.tx: Since the middle of the 19th century, first emerging in Berlin bourses, from earlier Mummelputz (“scarecrow, scary hooded figure”), equivalent to mummen (“to masquerade”) + Butz (“goblin”).

phrase:mein Name ist Hase.tx: Literally, “my name is Hase”, but often reinterpreted as “My name is hare”. because the underlying anecdote is not generally known. In 1854, Heidelberg student Victor von Hase gave his ID card to a fellow student, so the latter could flee to France; when the ID was later found, Hase was questioned by the university, and he replied: Mein Name ist Hase, ich verneine die Generalfragen, ich weiß von …

noun:Mamsell.tx: 17th century, from French mamzelle, contraction of mademoiselle.

noun:Mops.tx: Borrowed from Dutch mops (“pug”). Further origin unsettled. Possibly a malicious use of mop (“German; Fritz; Kraut”), an early variant of mof. Alternatively from mopperen (“to grumble”), earlier also moppen, to which compare regional German möppern. The latter is plausible given the seemingly grumpy face of the dog.

noun:Mandant.tx: Ultimatively from Latin mandāns, present active participle of mandō (“to grant”); perhaps via French mandant.

noun:Muttersöhnchen.tx: Compound of Mutter (“mother”) + Söhnchen (“diminutive of Sohn (little son)”).

noun:Myrrhe.tx: 16th-century relatinization of older Mirre, from Middle High German mirre, from Old High German mirra, myrra, from Ecclesiastical Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρᾱ (múrrhā), from a Semitic language.

noun:Mudder.tx: MUD + -er (or borrowed from English mudder with the same derivation)

noun:Melisse.tx: From the genus name translingual Melissa, from Ancient Greek μέλισσα (mélissa, “honey bee”), from μέλι (méli, “honey”).

noun:Maat.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German māt, māte, from Old Saxon gimato, of West Germanic origin, from Proto-Germanic *gamatjô, itself from *ga- (“together”) + *matjô, from *matiz (“food”). Related to English mate, Dutch maat.

noun:Missetat.tx: From Middle High German missetāt, from Old High German mistāt, missitāt (“misdeed”), from Proto-Germanic *missadēdiz < *missa- (“mis-”) + *dēdiz (“deed, act”). Compare Dutch misdaad, West Frisian misdied, English misdeed, Danish misdåd, Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐍃𐍃𐌰𐌳𐌴𐌸𐍃 (missadēþs). More at misdeed.

noun:Manie.tx: 16th century, from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía).

noun:Mäuschen.tx: From Maus (“mouse”) + -chen (diminutive suffix), literally “mousekin”. Doublet of Mäusken (the Low German form).

adj:muskulös.tx: Borrowed from French musculeux, from Latin mūsculōsus. By surface analysis, Muskul + -ös.

noun:Mischling.tx: Inherited from Middle High German mischelinc, equivalent to mischen (“to mix”) + -ling (“-ling”). Cognate with English mixling.

adj:mickrig.tx: Of dialectal origin, particularly found in eastern dialects of German Low German.

noun:Mumm.tx: Probably shortened from Latin animum, accusative singular of animus.

noun:Minderwertigkeitskomplex.tx: From Minderwertigkeit + -s- + Komplex. Coined by Austrian psychotherapist Alfred Adler in 1920.

adj:mutterseelenallein.tx: 18th century, from earlier mutterallein (16th c., literally “mother-alone”), which is either “as alone as a child in the womb” or more likely “as alone as a child bereft of its mother”. The contemporary form is equivalent to Mutterseele + -n- + allein, wherein the word Mutterseele (literally “mother soul”) is an emotive enhancement of Mutter (like the usual Menschenseele for Mensch). Discredited …

adj:musikalisch.tx: From Latin mūsicālis. By surface analysis, Musik + -alisch.

noun:Maki.tx: Borrowed from French maki, from Malagasy maky (“ring-tailed lemur”).

verb:martern.tx: From Middle High German martern, marteren, from Old High German martirōn, martarōn, martrōn.

verb:mitbringen.tx: mit- + bringen; cognate with Hunsrik mitbringe.

noun:Mongo.tx: Clipping of Mongoloider, from the adjective mongoloid. Compare Swedish mongo.

noun:Makulatur.tx: Ca. 1500, a learned borrowing from Latin maculātūra in the context of printing.

noun:Markgraf.tx: From Middle High German marcgrāve, from Old High German marcgrāvo. By surface analysis, Mark + Graf.

verb:muffen.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German muffen (“to have a moldy smell”), of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly related to modder (“mud”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“sediment”). However, compare Old High German *muff (“mold”).

noun:Muhme.tx: From Middle High German muome, from Old High German *muoma, from Proto-West Germanic *mōmā, from Proto-Germanic *mōmǭ (“mother, aunt”). Cognate with Yiddish מומע (mume), Middle English mome (“aunt, affectionate term for an older woman”), English mom (“mother”), Russian мама (mama, “mother”).

phrase:macht nichts.tx: Short for das macht nichts (literally “that makes nothing”).

verb:mauern.tx: From Middle High German mūren, from the root of Mauer (“wall”).

noun:Maraca.tx: Borrowed from Brazilian Portuguese maraca, derived from Old Tupi maraká or Paraguayan Guarani mbaraká (“rattle”).

verb:mitnehmen.tx: From mit- + nehmen; cognate with Hunsrik mitnemme.

noun:Mage.tx: From Middle High German māc, Old High German māc, from Proto-West Germanic *māg.

verb:mitspielen.tx: mit- + spielen; cognate with Hunsrik mitspiele

noun:Merlot.tx: From French, a diminutive of merle (“blackbird”).

noun:Metropolis.tx: Borrowed from Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis).

adj:mürbe.tx: From Old High German murwi, from Proto-Germanic *marwaz. Akin to English mellow, Dutch murw and Swedish mör.

noun:Magnum.tx: Ultimatively from magnus. Feminine gender could come from Flasche, Patrone.

adj:mulmig.tx: From archaic Mulm + -ig, related to mahlen.

adj:mühselig.tx: Equivalent to Mühe + selig. Derived from Middle High German müesal (“burden, vexation”) , müejesalic, müesalic (“tiring labor”). From Old High German muosal. Compare also armselig and trübselig

adv:mühselig.tx: Equivalent to Mühe + selig. Derived from Middle High German müesal (“burden, vexation”) , müejesalic, müesalic (“tiring labor”). From Old High German muosal. Compare also armselig and trübselig

noun:Menschenfuß.tx: From Middle High German menschenfuoz, menschenvuoz, equivalent to Mensch (“human”) + Fuß (“foot”).

noun:Mascara.tx: Borrowed from English mascara with a spelling pronunciation.

verb:munkeln.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German munkelen (“to speak in private”). Further origin unknown, possibly onomatopoeic, similar to mummeln.

pt: remind (someone of something) pressingly; warn (someone of something); urge (someone to do something necessary)
noun:Mahnmal.tx: mahnen (“remind (someone of something) pressingly; warn (someone of something); urge (someone to do something necessary)”) + Mal

noun:Mischpoke.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish משפּחה (mishpokhe), in turn from Hebrew משפחה (mishpakhá).

noun:Marille.tx: Borrowed from Italian armellino. Do not confuse with the nightshade Morelle and the cherry Morelle (“morello”), Schattenmorelle, which have been mixed up in dialects; an older form of this Marille word Ammarelle meant a kind of cherry.

noun:Mostrich.tx: Modification of Mostert, from Old French moustarde, from moust (“must”), from Latin mustum (“must; unfermented or partially fermented grape juice or wine”).

adj:methodisch.tx: From Latin methodicus, from Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós). Morphologically analyzable as Methode (“method”) + -isch.

adj:medikamentös.tx: Most likely borrowed from French médicamenteux, equivalent to Medikament + -ös.

verb:mampfen.tx: Originally "to speak with a full mouth," probably of imitative origin.

verb:müßigen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German müezigen, from Old High German muozīgen, from Proto-West Germanic *mōtīgijan.

noun:Moder.tx: From late Middle High German moder (“mold, swamp”), borrowed from Middle Low German modder, modde, mōde (“mud”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“dreg”), from Proto-Indo-European *múHtrom. Doublet of Modder (“mud”), a later borrowing. Cognate with Dutch modder.

noun:Muss.tx: Substantivization of muss (“must”), third-person singular present indicative of müssen (“to have to”).

noun:Maschendrahtzaun.tx: From Maschendraht + Zaun or Masche + -n- + Drahtzaun.

noun:Mähre.tx: From Middle High German meriche, merhe, from Old High German meriha, from Proto-West Germanic *marhijā, from Proto-Germanic *marhijō (“mare”), from *marhaz.

noun:Mikado.tx: Derived from Japanese. The game is named after the most valuable stick, which is called mikado (like the emperor of Japan).

verb:mitsingen.tx: mit- + singen; cognate with Hunsrik mitsinge

verb:mitziehen.tx: mit- + ziehen; cognate with Hunsrik mitziehe

adj:muffig.tx: The senses "smelly" and "grumpy" go back to different origins. The former pertains to Muff (“bad smell”) from Middle Low German muffen; the latter to Muffel (“grumpy person”), which is an Upper German dialect word of unknown origin. In contemporary German both senses often overlap (see below). It is therefore impossible to treat them as separate words anymore. Compare the same mixture of roots in muffelig.

noun:Münzgeld.tx: Münz(e) (“coin”) + Geld (“money”). Cognate with Dutch muntgeld.

adj:moppelig.tx: 20th century, from West Central German dialects. Perhaps eventually related with Mops, but probably not a direct derivative.

noun:Macker.tx: From German Low German Macker (“companion; guy”), first attested in 1771 and hence possibly borrowed from Dutch makker (“mate, fellow”) (1557). Further origin uncertain, but likely related to Old Saxon gimaco (“companion”), Old English maca, ġemaca (“companion, mate, wife, one suited to another, idem”), Old Norse maki (whence Swedish make (“husband”)), from Proto-Germanic *makkô, *gamakkô, *makô, …

noun:Meute.tx: 18th century, from French meute, from Old French meute.

noun:Mulle.tx: Compare German Molle (“beer glass; bed”) and also English moll.

verb:musizieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin mūsicāre (16th c.). Equivalent to Musik + -ieren (“-ise, -ify”).

noun:Marter.tx: Middle High German marter, from Old High German martira, from ecclesiastical Latin martyrium.

noun:Morphium.tx: Coined by Friedrich Sertürner in 1804, from Morpheus + -ium.

noun:Morast.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German mōras, an alteration of Middle Dutch maras on the basis of the predecessor of German Moor (“bog; moor”).

noun:Mär.tx: From Middle High German mære, from Old High German mārī, ultimately from the adjective māri (“well known, famous”), from Proto-West Germanic *mārī, from Proto-Germanic *mērijaz.

noun:Mistwetter.tx: Technically a compound of Mist (“dung”) + Wetter (“weather”). Mist! is a rather common interjection equivalent to English crap. However, the word is not freely prefixed to nouns, which makes it seem likely that Mistwetter is originally "misty weather", pertaining to Middle Low German mist (“mist”). The association with German Mist (“dung”) would thus be secondary. Compare, on the other hand, …

noun:Metaphysik.tx: From Latin metaphysica, from Medieval Greek μεταφυσική (metaphusikḗ). By surface analysis, meta- + Physik.

noun:Macke.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish מכּה (make, “plague, wound”), from Hebrew מַכָּה (maká, “blow, wound”), from הִכָּה (hiká, “to hit, to strike”).

noun:Männlein.tx: From Middle High German menlīn, mennelīn, from Old High German menlīn, mennilīn, mannilīn, equivalent to Mann + -lein. Compare English manling.

pt: to know of, be conscious of
noun:Mitwisser.tx: mitwissen (“to know of, be conscious of”) + -er (“-er”)

noun:Mahlstrom.tx: From Dutch maalstroom; analyzable as mahlen (“to grind”) + Strom (“stream”). Compare English maelstrom.

verb:mäkeln.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?]. The verb originally means “do business” and pertains to Makler (“broker”). It is not necessarily, however, the origin of this latter noun, whose attestations are significantly older. Rather it seems to be a back-formation. The further semantic development of the verb via “to haggle”, probably reinforced by unrelated Makel (“fault”).

noun:Matjes.tx: Shortened from Matjeshering, which is borrowed from Dutch maatjesharing, from Middle Dutch medykenshering (literally “maiden herring”), formed from the cognates of German Mädchen (“girl”) and Hering (“herring”). The word was borrowed into several European languages, though the common term in contemporary Dutch is nieuwe haring (“new herring”).

noun:Modder.tx: Borrowed from German Low German modder (“mud”), from Middle Low German modder (“mud”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz. Doublet of Moder (“moldiness”), which see for more.

noun:Mulde.tx: From Middle High German muolter, multer, mulde, from Old High German muoltra, mulda, from Latin mulctra (“milking pail”). The modern form with -d- and without final -r- is Central and Low German; compare also Middle Low German molde, molle.

verb:murksen.tx: Derived from Middle Low German morken (“to crush; to mash”). Hence also abmurksen (“to murder”). Probably related with morsch (“brittle”).

adj:mustergültig.tx: From Muster (“template; example”) + gültig (“valid”); by 1806 (as 18th-century musterhaft).

noun:Mehrwert.tx: Mehr (“increase, excess”) + wert (“worth, value”); cognate to English more + worth.

noun:Moschus.tx: From Medieval Latin moschus, alternative form of muscus, from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian [script needed] (mwšk' /⁠mušk⁠⁠/).

noun:Monokel.tx: Borrowed from French monocle, from Latin monoculus.

adj:mundtot.tx: Originally (17th century) a juridical term meaning “legally incapable”, in which mund- is the now obsolete word Middle High German munt (“protection, guardianship”), from Old High German munt, from Proto-Germanic *mundō. Later reanalyzed as Mund (“mouth”) + tot (“dead”) and semantically reinterpreted accordingly.

noun:Massenvernichtungswaffe.tx: From Masse + -n- + Vernichtung + -s- + Waffe, literally “mass annihiliation weapon”.

noun:Mouse.tx: Borrowed from English mouse. Doublet of Maus.

adj:mollig.tx: Originally student slang. Probably from Early New High German mollicht (“soft, relaxed”), from Latin mollis (“soft”).

noun:Morgengabe.tx: From Middle High German morgengābe, from Old High German morgangeba, Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō, equivalent to Morgen (“morning”) + Gabe (“gift”).

noun:Mufti.tx: Borrowed from Arabic مُفْتٍ (muftin), definite اَلْمُفْتِي (al-muftī), the active participle of أَفْتَى (ʔaftā, “to deliver a formal opinion”).

noun:Mäzen.tx: Borrowed from Latin Maecēnās (“literary patron”), from the name of Gaius Maecenas, Roman statesman and patron of Horace and Virgil.

adj:mannhaft.tx: From Middle High German manhaft. Equivalent to Mann + -haft.

adj:mannstoll.tx: Contraction of Middle High German mannes tol. Equivalent to Manns + toll.

noun:Maggi.tx: Named after Swiss entrepreneur and inventor Julius Maggi.

noun:Mungo.tx: Borrowed from English mungos, a variant form of mongoose. The final s was mistaken for an indicator of plurality leading to the back-formation of the German singular. Doublet of Manguste.

noun:Muff.tx: From older Muffel, from Dutch muffel, from Old French moufle, Medieval Latin muffula.

noun:Merk.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German merk, from Old Saxon *merk, *merik, from Proto-West Germanic *marik.

noun:Matura.tx: Borrowed from New Latin exāmina mātūra.

noun:Meisterstück.tx: From Meister (“master”) + Stück (“piece”). Compare Dutch meesterstuk.

noun:Macherin.tx: From Middle High German macherinne. Equivalent to Macher + -in.

noun:Machtergreifung.tx: Macht (“power”) + Ergreifung (“seizure”), (from ergreifen (“seize”) + -ung (resultative verbal noun)), 19th century.

noun:Mittsommer.tx: From Middle High German mittesummer, equivalent to mitt- + Sommer. Compare English midsummer.

verb:monieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin monēre, from moneō (“to warn, advise”). Compare English admonish, monitor.

noun:Mitesser.tx: Calque of Latin comedō, from mitessen + -er.

noun:Monstrum.tx: Latin mōnstrum, 16th c. Doublet of Monster.

noun:Matze.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish מצה (matse), from Hebrew מַצָּה (matsá).

noun:Mastvieh.tx: Compound of mästen (“to fatten”) + Vieh (“livestock”). Compare Dutch mestvee.

noun:Mannweib.tx: Calque of Ancient Greek ἀνδρόγυνος (andrógunos), Mann + Weib.

verb:mittun.tx: From mit- + tun. Cognate with Dutch meedoen, Hunsrik mitdun.

noun:Mundraub.tx: 18th century, from Mund (“mouth”) + Raub (“robbery”), at first in northern authors after Middle Low German mundrôf (early 16th c.).

noun:Mürbeteig.tx: Affix of mürbe (“crumbly”) + Teig (“dough”). Cognate with Swedish mördeg.

phrase:mit jemandem ist nicht gut Kirsch.tx: Literally, “eating cherries is not good with someone”.

noun:Mummenschanz.tx: Middle High German mummen (“game of chance”, noun) (compare Old French momon) and Middle High German schanze (“chance”).

noun:Mensur.tx: Borrowed from Latin mēnsūra (“measure”). In the context of fencing, the term originally denoted the distance that two fencers had to stand from one another.

noun:Monobraue.tx: From mono- + Braue (“brow”), most probably a calque of English monobrow.

noun:Moritat.tx: Probably a corruption of Mordtat, Mord + Tat.

intj:Mannomann.tx: Univerbation of Mann + oh + Mann, an emphatic repetition of the interjection Mann (“(Oh) man!”).

noun:Müßiggänger.tx: Inherited from Middle High German müeʒicgenger. By surface analysis, Müßiggang + -er.

noun:Myrte.tx: 16th-century relatinization of older Mirtel, Mirten, from Middle High German mirtel, from Old High German mirtil, from Latin myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).

noun:Mauschel.tx: From Yiddish משהלע (Moyshele), diminutive of Hebrew משה (Moshe, “Moses”).

verb:mauscheln.tx: Mauschel + -en, from Yiddish, influenced by Rotwelsch.

noun:Misanthrop.tx: Learned borrowing from French misanthrope, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μισάνθρωπος (misánthrōpos).

noun:Maharadscha.tx: 19th century, from English maharaja, from Hindi महाराजा (mahārājā), from Sanskrit महाराज (mahārāja).

noun:Medaillenspiegel.tx: From Medaille (“medal”) + Spiegel (“chart, table, register”, literally “mirror”).

noun:Meerschwein.tx: From Middle High German merswīn, from Old High German meriswīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mariswīn, from Proto-Germanic *mariswīną; equivalent to Meer + Schwein. Compare archaic English mereswine.

verb:metzeln.tx: From late Middle High German metzelen, from Medieval Latin macellare (“slaughter”), from Latin macellum (“meat, meat market”).

noun:Muffe.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun:Moorhuhn.tx: Calque of English moorhen, Moor (“fen, moor”) + Huhn (“hen”).
